extracted.intended_audience: poets, translators, writers, and students of literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and critical guidance on poetic diction, translation, taste, and pedagogy drawn from literary criticism and footnotes; aimed at informing how to write, translate, judge, and teach poetry/prose. Emphasises language-specific constraints, study of models, and proper enunciation/usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature or immoderate authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: “With the greatest possible solicitude avoid authorship. Too early or immoderately employed, it makes the head waste and the heart empty; even were there no other worse consequences. A person, who reads only to print, to all probability reads amiss; and he, who sends away through the pen and the press every thought, the moment it occurs to him, will in a short time have sent all away, and will become a mere journeyman of the printing-office, a compositor.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not publish or force authorship too early or excessively; cultivate thoughts by re-absorbing and 're-secreting' them to maintain intellectual vigour. Reading only for the sake of printing leads to bad reading; habitual immediate publication dissipates mental resources and craftsmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquire good taste by studying the best models
rubrics_metrics.description: “Good taste must be acquired, and like all other good things, is the result of thought and the submissive study of the best models.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To form 'good taste' actively study canonical works. Use the established masters (those whose reputation has been matured into fame) as primary exemplars; taste is learned through deliberate attention to enduring models rather than through instinct alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical reputation as a guide to the 'best' works
rubrics_metrics.description: “Presume those to be the best, the reputation of which has been matured into fame by the consent of ages.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When uncertain which models to study or imitate, favour works that have stood the test of time. The 'consent of ages' and long-established reputation are practical heuristics for selecting exemplary literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect language-specific genius when translating
rubrics_metrics.description: “The attempt were not encouraged by the different genius of the English mind and language, which demands a denser body of thought as the condition of a high polish, than the Italian.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before translating, consider whether the source-language poetic idiom maps naturally onto the target language. Differences in national 'genius' and idiom (e.g., Italian's clear separation of poetic and prose registers, English's demand for denser thought) may render literal translation inappropriate or ineffective; translation strategy must account for these differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve register distinctions between poetry and prose
rubrics_metrics.description: “I cannot but deem it likewise an advantage in the Italian tongue, in many other respects inferior to our own, that the language of poetry is more distinct from that of prose than with us.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain appropriate register shifts: poetic diction should differ noticeably from prose diction in tone and phrasing. If the target language lacks a strong separate poetic register, the translator or poet must work deliberately to create or compensate for that distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of extending a word's meaning beyond its original signification
rubrics_metrics.description: “I object to any extension of its meaning, because the word is already more equivocal than might be wished... It can therefore be preserved from obscurity only by keeping the original signification full in the mind.” (example: the word 'scene')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid careless semantic broadening of key theatrical/literary terms (e.g., 'scene'). Preserve original or historically grounded senses to prevent equivocality and obscurity; when repurposing terms, be mindful of potential ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain poetic diction and avoid prose-like versification
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge notes that approximation of prose in verse is often 'sedulously and on system guarded against' and praises authors who avoid prose-phrasing in poetry, while acknowledging rare, justified exceptions tied to narrator voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep verse distinctively poetic in diction and rhythm; avoid inserting ordinary conversational constructions that make lines read like prose unless the voice or dramatic purpose explicitly calls for it (e.g., a character's spoken register).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive or mechanical repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: “This sort of repetition is one of this writer's peculiarities, and there is scarce a page which does not furnish one or more instances...” (lists many repeated phrases as examples)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat frequent, unvaried repetition as a stylistic fault unless it serves a deliberate rhetorical, rhythmic, or thematic purpose. Identify and edit redundancies that do not contribute meaningfully to tone or emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure metaphors and images are proper to the context
rubrics_metrics.description: On a metaphor from Shakespeare about a stag: where in the supposed position of Bertram the metaphor, 'if not false, loses all the propriety of the original.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate metaphors for situational appropriateness: a vivid image in its original scene can become strained or improper when transposed. Keep metaphors true to the physical or psychological conditions that justify them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider language-specific structural resources (compounding, inflections) for concision and pictorial force
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of German's 'facility and force of compound epithets' and the power of German and Greek to condense meaning by compounds and inflections, contrasted with English's reliance on Latin-derived forms and the lack of certain prefixes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or translating, be conscious of what each language can express succinctly through compounds or inflections. Use or simulate such devices when possible to preserve unity and simultaneousness of impression; conversely, account for loss of condensation when moving into a language less capable of single-word condensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach reading and recitation appropriate to the act (reading ≠ speaking/singing)
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is no less an error in teachers... to enforce the necessity of reading as they would talk. In order to cure them of singing... the child is made to repeat the words with his eyes from off the book; and then, indeed, his tones resemble talking... two acts are accompanied with widely different feelings, so must they justify different modes of enunciation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In pedagogy and performance training, distinguish between spoken conversation, singing, and recited reading. Do not mechanically force spoken delivery habits onto reading aloud; cultivate modes of enunciation suited to the distinct psychological acts and feelings involved. Avoid punitive or dehumanizing methods (e.g., the criticized Lancaster practice) that harm natural expression.
